q1: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2: SELECT C1.CUSTOMER_ID FROM (SELECT DISTINCT CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY FROM CUSTOMER) AS C1 GROUP BY C1.CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(C1.PRODUCT_KEY)=(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PRODUCT)
q1_prompt_sql: SELECT CUSTOMER_ID FROM CUSTOMER GROUP BY 1 HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) FROM PRODUCT)
q2_prompt_sql: SELECT C1.CUSTOMER_ID FROM (SELECT DISTINCT CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY FROM CUSTOMER) AS C1 GROUP BY C1.CUSTOMER_ID HAVING COUNT(C1.PRODUCT_KEY)=(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM PRODUCT)
counterexample:
INSERT INTO PRODUCT (PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1), (2), (3);
INSERT INTO CUSTOMER (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) VALUES (1, 1), (1, 1), (1, 2);
explanation: Q1 and Q2 are not semantically equivalent. Q1 compares the count of distinct product keys per customer to the total distinct product keys in the PRODUCT table, while Q2 compares the count of product keys per customer (after deduplication of customer-product pairs) to the total number of rows in the PRODUCT table. These two conditions are not equivalent, especially when there are duplicate customer-product pairs in the CUSTOMER table.
counterexample_dsp: A scenario where the CUSTOMER table has duplicate (CUSTOMER_ID, PRODUCT_KEY) pairs and the PRODUCT table has more rows than distinct product keys (though in reality, since PRODUCT_KEY is the primary key, all are distinct). This highlights the difference in COUNT(DISTINCT PRODUCT_KEY) vs COUNT(*).
